rows: Birds can see a light flicker 40 to 140 times a second, and the fastest fliers are at the top of that range. People see flicker up to about 60 times a second. This view runs slowly and then jumps ahead to suggest the difference.
Most birds see half as much detail as people do, or less.

A starling, a blue tit and a blackbird have a short-wave cone that peaks in the ultraviolet, between 360 and 375 nanometers, and gulls have the same type. A mallard, a pigeon and a chicken have the violet type instead, which peaks between 410 and 420. If you are a duck or a vulture, you very likely see little ultraviolet, and if you are a songbird or a gull, you very likely see it.
Eyes on the sides of the head probably give a wide view. This part of the view is a guess.

rows: A zebra finch takes in about 300 degrees around its head, with only about 10 degrees of overlap straight ahead. You very likely see nearly all the way around you, with a gap behind your head.

A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart. A house sparrow reads 4.9, a domestic chicken about 7, an eastern towhee 8.4, an eastern meadowlark 10.3 and a rock pigeon 12.8. You very likely see less fine detail than a human does.

If you are a starling, a house sparrow or a house finch, each of your eyes holds one small area where the cells pack at more than 20,000 per square millimeter. If you are a pigeon, you look at distant things with your foveas and at food near your feet with a separate area of the retina.

A starling's four cone pigments peak at 362, 449, 504 and 563 nanometers, and a blackbird, a blue tit and a canary agree within about ten nanometers. You very likely sense four primary colors, one of them ultraviolet, where a human senses three.

If you are a rock pigeon, your shortest-wave cones peak near 409 nanometers, in the violet. If you are a domestic chicken, they peak near 419. A pigeon's sensitivity still reaches well into the ultraviolet below 400 nanometers.

A blue tit, a collared flycatcher and a pied flycatcher tell flickering light from steady light up to 130 to 145 times a second, where a human stops at about 60. A pigeon manages about 77 and a chicken about 72. You very likely follow fast motion in finer steps than a human does.

Nobody has measured how fast sharpness falls from the sharp spot toward the edge of a bird's picture, and nobody can say how ultraviolet looks to a bird. The size of that fall and how much of the blue is read as ultraviolet are guesses.
Nobody has measured some parts of how you see, so they are guesses.

Birds can see a light flicker 40 to 140 times a second, and the fastest fliers are at the top of that range. People see flicker up to about 60 times a second. This view runs slowly and then jumps ahead to suggest the difference.
Most birds see half as much detail as people do, or less.
Eyes on the sides of the head probably give a wide view. This part of the view is a guess.

On this trial a songbird's four colour classes are drawn three at a time, ultraviolet in the bluest slot; dragging across the picture with the wheel turns which three are shown. Two of the four peaks are the app's guesses.

With motion allowed, the picture holds still in the world between quick catches, as a bird's head does while its body moves. How long it holds and how far it lets the phone turn are the app's guesses.

Many songbirds and pigeons sense the direction of the earth's magnetic field through their eyes, and the sense fails in red or yellow light. With &draw=grain or &draw=tide and the motion sensors on, the picture carries a texture tied to magnetic north that melts in warm light. The drawing is the app's.
